title: Sultanate of Oman
capsule: The Sultanate of Oman traces its modern lineage to the Al Bu Said dynasty founded by Ahmad ibn Said in 1744, who expelled Persian forces from Muscat and unified the coastal and interior factions. Under Said ibn Sultan (r. 1806–1856) the sultanate built a maritime empire linking Muscat to Zanzibar, Mombasa, and Gwadar, making it the dominant commercial power on the western Indian Ocean littoral. After Said's death the empire was partitioned between Oman (Muscat) and Zanzibar; the interior Imamate repeatedly challenged coastal Al Bu Said authority, and the sultanate only achieved full territorial control after suppressing the Jebel Akhdar rebellion in 1959, with Qaboos ibn Said's 1970 coup modernizing the state into the present-day Sultanate of Oman.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Coastal Oman's administrative extent is documented through Portuguese, British, and local Arabic sources; the boundaries with interior tribal confederacies and the shifting Imamate in the Hajar Mountains are poorly demarcated and subject to dispute through the mid-20th century.
